composition.story: A language model writes fluent text but doesn't know what people prefer. Follow one prompt: the model drafts answers, humans rank them, a reward model learns those rankings, and then the reward model, not people, scores answers while reinforcement learning nudges the model toward higher scores.

aha.observation: Humans only train the scorer. The reward model then grades answers for them, so reinforcement learning can shift the policy toward preferred answers.

controls.label: Step
controls.presentation: Previous / Next buttons; arrow keys also move between steps

states.label: Pretrained policy
states.sentence: The pretrained policy model predicts fluent text, but nothing yet tells it which answers people prefer.
states.why: This is the gap RLHF fills: fluent is not the same as preferred.

states.label: Sample answers
states.sentence: For one prompt, the policy model writes several different candidate answers.
states.why: Different samples give people something to compare.

states.label: Humans rank
states.sentence: Human raters rank the candidate answers from best to worst. Comparing is easier than writing ideal answers.
states.why: Rankings are the only place human preference enters.

states.label: Train reward model
states.sentence: The reward model trains to give higher scores to answers that humans ranked higher.
states.why: Human judgment is now compressed into a model that can score any answer.

states.label: Score and update
states.sentence: The reward model now scores new answers with no humans. The RL update shifts the policy toward higher-scoring answers.
states.why: Automatic scoring is what lets reinforcement learning run on huge numbers of samples.
